Jupiter. Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the solar system, a gas giant with a mass greater than all other planets combined. Named after the king of Roman gods, it orbits the Sun every twelve Earth years and has long been one of the most prominent objects in the night sky. Its dramatic appearance—dark bands and bright zones, whirling storms, and a distinctive Great Red Spot—makes it a cornerstone of planetary science and a primary target for space exploration.

Jupiter is a gas giant, composed mainly of hydrogen and helium with no solid surface. Its atmosphere displays violent jet streams and dynamic cloud systems.

The Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has raged for at least three hundred fifty years, visible through modest telescopes.

Jupiter has at least ninety-five known moons, including the four Galilean moons—Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto—discovered by Galileo Galilei in sixteen-ten.

Io is volcanically active and geologically turbulent. Europa harbors a subsurface ocean under its icy crust, making it a prime candidate in the search for extraterrestrial life.

The planet's magnetosphere is the strongest in the solar system, creating hazardous radiation belts.

Jupiter's rapid rotation—one day lasts roughly ten hours—flattens it visibly at the poles, a shape called an oblate spheroid.

The planet lies just outside the asteroid belt. Gravitational interactions with Jupiter are thought to have shaped the asteroid belt's architecture.
